summary: The Path Computation Element (PCE) is a core component of software-defined networking. This document specifies Path Computation Element Communication Protocol (PCEP) procedures and extensions for using the PCE as a central controller (PCECC) that provisions labels along the path of a static Label Switched Path, so that a central server can download label-forwarding entries to each device on the path.

plainLanguage.summary: In a traditional network, each router along a path decides for itself which label to use for the next hop. This document lets one central server, the Path Computation Element, make that decision for every router and send each one its instruction. The routers then confirm that they installed it.

subtitle: How a central PCE server can tell every router on a static MPLS path which labels to use.

tldr.problem: A Path Computation Element can work out a path through a network, but telling every router along that path which label to use is still a distributed job that a central controller would rather do in one place.
tldr.mechanism: The document adds a Central Controller Instruction object to PCEP and a new path setup type, so that the PCE sends a PCInitiate message to each router on the path with the label instruction for that hop, and the router acknowledges with a PCRpt message.
tldr.outcome: Labels along a static label switched path can be provisioned from one central controller while the existing stateful PCE mechanisms keep working, and the document also defines the error codes, the cleanup and update procedures, and the security limits of the arrangement.

today: RFC 9050 is a Proposed Standard, and it was later updated by RFC 9756, which adjusted the IANA registration procedures for PCEP numbers and allowed experimental error codes. The document itself leaves the Segment Routing version of the central controller to separate work, so the basic mode described here is the static label switched path case.

sections.title: Why a PCE as a Central Controller
sections.content:
The Path Computation Element (PCE) was built to take the path computation work away from routers in an MPLS traffic-engineered network. It computes paths for traffic across the network and updates them when the network or the traffic changes. Over time its role grew to cover other uses, delegated control and PCE-initiated use of network resources.

Software-Defined Networking (SDN) means separating the control elements from the forwarding components, so that software in a centralized system, called a controller, can program the devices in the network to behave in specific ways. An SDN architecture needs a component that plans how the network's resources will be used and how the devices will be programmed. That is the function of a PCE.

In early PCE implementations the PCE derived paths for MPLS label switched paths, the paths were requested by network elements known as Path Computation Clients (PCCs), and the results were supplied to those elements over the Path Computation Element Communication Protocol (PCEP). SDN is broader than signalled MPLS and GMPLS traffic engineering, and PCEP has been proposed as a control protocol for such environments so that the PCE can act as a full central controller.

RFC 8283 introduces the architecture for the PCE as a central controller and examines PCEP as a Southbound Interface. This document specifies the procedures and PCEP extensions for using the PCE as the central controller for static LSPs, where the LSP is provisioned as explicit label instructions at each hop on the end-to-end path. Each router along the path must be told what label-forwarding instruction to program and what resources to reserve, and the controller uses PCEP to talk to every one of them.

The document focuses on the static LSP case, which it calls the basic PCECC mode, but the mechanisms and encodings are specified so that extensions for other cases are easy to add. The Segment Routing extensions, for instance, are written elsewhere.
sections.plainLanguage: A Path Computation Element is a server that works out routes through a network. This document lets that server go further and also program the routers, sending each one the exact label to use. It concentrates the control of a path in one place instead of leaving it spread across the routers on that path.

sections.title: Basic PCECC Mode and the Label Space
sections.content:
In the basic PCECC mode, LSPs are provisioned as explicit label instructions at each hop on the end-to-end path. Every router along the path has to be told what label-forwarding instruction to program and what resources to reserve, and the controller uses PCEP to communicate with each router on the path.

The PCE-based controller takes responsibility for managing some part of the MPLS label space for each router it controls, and may take a wider responsibility for partitioning the label space and allocating different parts for different uses. The PCC MUST NOT make allocations from the label space set aside for the PCE, so that label allocations do not overlap or collide. It is RECOMMENDED that the PCE makes allocations from the space set aside for it for all nodes along the path. This document assumes that the exclusive label range used by a PCE is known and set on both PCEP peers; a future extension could add the ability to advertise that range over PCEP.

The document also allows the opposite arrangement, where the label space is maintained by the PCC and the labels are allocated by it. In that case the PCE requests the allocation from the PCC.

Five requirements are listed for anyone designing a PCECC-based solution: a PCEP speaker must be able to advertise its PCECC capability to its peers; it needs a means to identify PCECC-based LSPs in the PCEP messages; the procedures must allow for PCC-based label allocations; they must provide a means to update or clean up label entries downloaded to the PCC; and they must provide a means to synchronize the labels between the PCE and the PCC.
sections.plainLanguage: The labels a router may use are split into a part the central server owns and the rest. The server is told to pick labels only from its own part, so two things never end up using the same label. The document also allows the opposite split, where the router picks its own label and tells the server which one it chose.

sections.title: Advertising the Capability
sections.content:
During the PCEP initialization phase, the two speakers, the PCE and the PCC, advertise their support for and willingness to use the PCECC extensions with three elements in the OPEN message.

  • A new Path Setup Type, PST, listed in the PATH-SETUP-TYPE-CAPABILITY TLV to indicate support for the PCECC extensions. The value 2 means the traffic engineering path is set up using PCECC mode.
  • A new PCECC-CAPABILITY sub-TLV inside the PATH-SETUP-TYPE-CAPABILITY TLV, with the L bit set to 1, to indicate a willingness to handle the Central Controller Instructions for label download.
  • The STATEFUL-PCE-CAPABILITY TLV from RFC 8231, with the I flag set as RFC 8281 requires.

The PCECC-CAPABILITY sub-TLV is an optional TLV for use in the OPEN object when the Path Setup Type list includes PCECC Path Setup Type 2. It has a type of 1 and a fixed length of 4 octets, and its value is a single 32-bit Flags field. The L bit, the Label bit, indicates that the speaker will support and is willing to handle the PCECC-based Central Controller Instructions for label download. The bit MUST be set to 1 by both a PCC and a PCE for the PCECC label download and report on a PCEP session. Unassigned bits MUST be set to 0 on transmission and MUST be ignored on receipt.

The rules are strict about mismatches. If the PCECC-CAPABILITY sub-TLV is advertised but the STATEFUL-PCE-CAPABILITY TLV is missing, or is present without the I flag, the receiver MUST send a PCErr message with Error-Type 19 (Invalid Operation) and Error-value 17 (Stateful PCE capability was not advertised) and MUST terminate the session. If a speaker receives the PATH-SETUP-TYPE-CAPABILITY TLV with the PCECC path setup type but without the PCECC-CAPABILITY sub-TLV, it MUST send a PCErr message with Error-Type 10 (Reception of an invalid object) and Error-value 33 (Missing PCECC Capability sub-TLV) and MUST terminate the session. The PCECC-CAPABILITY sub-TLV MUST NOT be used without the corresponding path setup type being listed; if it appears without it, it MUST be ignored.

If one or both speakers have not indicated support and willingness to use the PCECC extensions, the extensions MUST NOT be used. If a PCECC operation is attempted anyway, the receiver of the message MUST send a PCErr message with Error-Type 19 and Error-value 16 (Attempted PCECC operations when PCECC capability was not advertised) and MUST terminate the PCEP session.

A legacy PCEP speaker that does not recognize the PCECC-CAPABILITY sub-TLV ignores it. On receipt of an unsupported path setup type in a Request Parameter or Stateful PCE Request Parameter object, it sends a PCErr message with Error-Type 21 (Invalid traffic engineering path setup type) and Error-value 1 (Unsupported path setup type) and terminates the session.
sections.plainLanguage: Before anything else happens, the server and the router each say in the opening message whether they are willing to work this way. If either side stays silent, neither may use the new procedures, and an attempt to do so ends the session with an error.

sections.title: Setting Up a PCECC Path
sections.content:
A PCEP message consists of a common header followed by a variable-length body made of a set of objects that are either mandatory or optional. An object is mandatory in a message when it must be included for the message to be valid, and each message type has rules defining the set of objects it may carry. The document extends three existing PCEP messages: PCInitiate to set up a PCE-initiated LSP and to carry the Central Controller Instructions, PCRpt to report state and to report the instructions received, and PCUpd to send LSP updates.

Every PCEP message that pertains to a PCECC MUST include the PATH-SETUP-TYPE TLV in the Stateful PCE Request Parameter object with the path setup type set to 2, so that the PCECC LSP is clearly identified.

In the PCE-initiated case the PCE sends a PCInitiate message with the path setup type set to 2 to the ingress PCC. The label-forwarding instructions are sent after the initial PCInitiate and PCRpt exchange with the ingress PCC, so that the PCEP-specific identifier for the LSP, the PLSP-ID, and the other LSP identifiers can be obtained from the ingress and included in the instructions that follow.

An LSP-IDENTIFIERS TLV MUST be included for PCECC LSPs; it uniquely identifies the LSP in the network. The fields are described for RSVP-signalled LSPs but apply to the PCECC LSP as well. The LSP object is included in the Central Controller Instruction to identify the PCECC LSP for that instruction. The PLSP-ID is the original identifier used by the ingress PCC, so a transit or egress router could have several instructions with the same PLSP-ID; the PLSP-ID together with the source in the LSP-IDENTIFIERS TLV MUST be unique. The PLSP-ID is included for maintainability reasons, to ease debugging. The LSP object could also include the SPEAKER-ENTITY-ID TLV to identify the PCE that initiated the instructions. The CC-ID is unique within each PCEP session.

On receipt of the PCInitiate message the PCC responds with a PCRpt message with the status set to Going-up and carrying the assigned PLSP-ID, and the ingress PCC sets the Delegate flag and the Create flag in the LSP object. The PCE then assigns labels along the path and sets up the path by sending a PCInitiate message to each node along the path. Each node responds with a PCRpt message to acknowledge the instruction, and those reports carry the CCI and LSP objects.

The role of a node is visible in the instructions it receives. The ingress node receives one CCI object with the out-label bit set. A transit node receives two, the in-label one without the bit set and the out-label one with it set. The egress node receives one without the bit set. Once the label operations are complete the PCE MUST send a PCUpd message to the ingress PCC, with the Delegate flag set. The PCECC LSPs are considered to be up by default on receipt of that message. The ingress may further deploy a data-plane check and report the status back with a PCRpt message to make sure the right label instructions are in place and the path is ready to carry traffic; the exact mechanism is out of scope.

In the PCC-initiated case the PCC delegates the LSP by sending a PCRpt message with the path setup type set for PCECC and the Delegate flag set in the LSP object. The PCE SHOULD then calculate the path, assign labels along it and set up the path by sending a PCInitiate message to each node along the path. PCECC LSPs MUST be delegated to a PCE at all times.
sections.plainLanguage: The server first asks the entry router to start the path, and the entry router replies with an identifier for it. The server then walks down the path, sending each router the label instruction for that hop and getting an acknowledgement back from each. When the whole path is in place, the server sends a final update that marks the path as up.

sections.title: The CCI Object and the Message Bodies
sections.content:
The CCI object is used by the PCE to specify the forwarding instructions, which in this document are label instructions, to the PCC. It MAY be carried within a PCInitiate or PCRpt message for label download and report. The CCI Object-Class is 44 and the CCI Object-Type is 1 for the MPLS label.

The object carries a CC-ID, a 32-bit PCEP-specific identifier for the instruction. The PCE creates a CC-ID for each instruction; the value is unique within the scope of the PCE and is constant for the lifetime of a PCEP session. The values 0 and 0xFFFFFFFF are reserved and MUST NOT be used. The CC-ID is a transient numeric identifier, so the security advice on assigning such identifiers applies.

Reserved1 is a 16-bit field that is set to zero while sending and ignored on receipt. The Flags field is 16 bits and carries information about the instruction. Two flag bits are defined. The O bit, the out-label bit, set to 1 means the label is the out-label, and it is then mandatory to encode the next-hop information with Address TLVs in the CCI object; when the bit is not set the label is the in-label, and encoding the local interface information is optional. The C bit, the PCC allocation bit, set to 1 means the label allocation needs to be done by the PCC; a PCE sets it to request the PCC to make an allocation from its label space, and a PCC sets it to indicate that it has allocated the label and is reporting it. All unassigned bits MUST be set to zero at transmission and ignored at receipt.

The Label field is 20 bits and carries the label information. Reserved2 is 12 bits, set to zero while sending and ignored on receipt. Optional TLVs may follow.

The Address TLVs are the IPV4-ADDRESS, IPV6-ADDRESS and UNNUMBERED-ENDPOINT TLVs that RFC 8779 defines for Generalized Endpoint. They associate next-hop information with an outgoing label and local interface information with an incoming label. The next-hop information must be a directly connected IP address or interface. If the PCC cannot resolve it, it MUST reject the instruction and respond with a PCErr message with Error-Type 31 (PCECC failure) and Error-value 5 (Invalid next-hop information).

When a PCInitiate message is used for the instructions, the SRP, LSP and CCI objects MUST all be present. A missing SRP object means the PCC MUST send a PCErr message with Error-Type 6 (Mandatory Object missing) and Error-value 10 (SRP object missing); a missing LSP object means Error-value 8 (LSP object missing); and a missing CCI object means Error-value 17 (CCI object missing). More than one CCI object MAY be included in the PCInitiate message for a transit router. To clean up entries, the R, remove, bit MUST be set in the SRP object alongside the LSP and CCI objects.

The CCI object received at the ingress node MUST have the O bit set and the one at the egress MUST have it unset. If this is not the case the PCC MUST send a PCErr message with Error-Type 31 and Error-value 3 (Invalid CCI), and other CCI objects present MUST be ignored. For a point-to-point LSP setup at the transit router, two CCI objects are expected, one with the O bit set and one without; if the transit router did not receive two such objects it MUST send a PCErr message with Error-Type 31 and Error-value 3. The ingress, egress or transit role of the PCC is identified from the ingress and egress IP addresses encoded in the LSP-IDENTIFIERS TLV.

When a PCRpt message reports the instructions, the LSP and CCI objects MUST be present, with the same missing-object error values. Two CCI objects can be included in a PCRpt message for a transit router.
sections.plainLanguage: Each label instruction is a small object with an identifying number, a couple of flags and a 20-bit label field. One flag says whether the label is the one coming in or the one going out, and the other says whether the router should pick the label itself. The next-hop address travels in the same object.

sections.title: Cleanup, Updates and Error Reporting
sections.content:
To delete a PCECC LSP the PCE sends instructions by PCInitiate message to each node along the path to clean up the label-forwarding instruction, with the R flag set in the SRP object to signal the deletion. If the PCC receives such a message but does not recognize the label in the CCI, it MUST generate a PCErr message with Error-Type 19 (Invalid operation) and Error-value 18 (Unknown Label) and MUST include the SRP object to specify the error is for the corresponding label cleanup. Following the removal the PCC MUST send a PCRpt message, whose SRP object MUST include the SRP-ID-number from the PCInitiate message that triggered the removal, and the R flag in the SRP object MUST be set.

An update is done by the make-before-break procedure. The controller first updates the new label instructions based on the updated path, then informs the ingress to switch traffic, and only then cleans up the former instructions. New CC-IDs identify the updated instructions, while the identifiers in the LSP object uniquely identify the existing LSP. Once the new instructions are downloaded the PCE updates the new path at the ingress, which triggers the traffic switch; the ingress PCC acknowledges with a PCRpt message, and on receipt of it the PCE does the cleanup operation for the former LSP. Modified PCECC LSPs are considered to be up by default.

A new PCE can gain control over an orphaned LSP, and for a PCECC LSP the new PCE MUST also gain control over the instructions in the same way, by sending a PCInitiate message that includes the SRP, LSP and CCI objects and carries the CC-ID and PLSP-ID identifying the instructions it wants to take control of. The State Timeout Interval timer ensures that a PCE crash does not result in immediate disruption of the services using PCE-initiated LSPs. The instructions are not removed immediately on PCE failure either; they are cleaned up when the timer expires, which allows network cleanup without manual intervention. The PCC MUST support the removal of CCI as one of the behaviours applied on expiration of that timer.

The purpose of synchronization is to make sure the PCE's view of the instructions matches the PCC's label allocation. It is performed as part of the LSP state synchronization: the PCC reports the state of its LSPs to the PCE with PCRpt messages, and the PCE initiates any missing LSPs and removes any that are not wanted. The same messages and procedures are used for the instructions, with the PCRpt message including the CCI and the LSP object. The PCE then removes any unwanted instructions or initiates any missing ones.

The PCE can ask the PCC to allocate the label by setting the C flag in the CCI object to 1. The PCC MUST try to allocate the label and MUST report to the PCE with a PCRpt or PCErr message. A label value of 0 with the C flag set means the PCE is requesting the allocation; a label value of n with the C flag set means the PCE requests that specific value. If the allocation succeeds the PCC MUST report it with a PCRpt message carrying the CCI object. If the label value is invalid the PCC MUST send a PCErr message with Error-Type 31 and Error-value 3 (Invalid CCI). If it is valid but the PCC cannot allocate it, Error-value 4 (Unable to allocate the specified CCI). If the PCC wants to withdraw or modify a label it previously assigned, it MUST send a PCRpt message with no label or with the new label value in the CCI object, and the PCE then triggers the label cleanup of the older label.
sections.plainLanguage: When a path is torn down the server tells each router to remove the label it installed, and each router confirms. When a path changes the server installs the new labels first, moves the traffic, and only then removes the old ones, so the path never breaks in the middle. If the server dies, the instructions stay in place until a timer expires.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security considerations for a PCE-based controller differ from those for any other PCE system, because the operation relies heavily on the use and security of PCEP. The security features discussed in RFC 5440 and the additional mechanisms described in RFC 8253 apply. The architecture of a central controller has its own weaknesses, such as a central point of failure, denial of service, and a focus for interception and modification of messages sent to individual network elements. In PCECC operations the PCEP sessions are also required to the internal routers, which increases the session management resources needed at the PCE.

RFC 8253 specifies support for Transport Layer Security in PCEP, providing peer authentication, message encryption and integrity, and mechanisms for associating peer identities with different levels of access or authoritativeness through an attribute in X.509 certificates or a local policy with an accept list of certificates. That can be used to check the authority for the PCECC operations.

With this extension the PCE has complete control over the PCC to download and remove labels, and can cause the LSPs to behave inappropriately and have a major impact on the network. As a general precaution it is RECOMMENDED that the PCEP extension be activated on mutually authenticated and encrypted sessions across PCEs and PCCs belonging to the same administrative authority, using TLS, following the recommendations and best current practices in BCP 195.

An attacker may flood the PCC with PCECC-related messages at a rate that exceeds either the PCC's ability to process them or the network's ability to send them, either by spoofing messages or by compromising the PCE itself. The rate-limiting mechanism of RFC 8281 protects the PCC and can be used for the PCECC operations as well. A PCC also needs to check whether the label in the CCI object is in the range set aside for the PCE; otherwise it MUST send a PCErr message with Error-Type 31 and Error-value 1 (Label out of range).

A malicious PCC is a second concern. The mechanism requires the PCE to keep the instructions it downloads, and to rely on the PCC responding with either an acknowledgement or an error message to request an LSP instantiation. That is an extra attack surface, because the PCE must keep a replica of the instructions for each PCC. It is RECOMMENDED that PCE implementations put a limit on the resources a single PCC can occupy, and RFC 8231 provides a notification mechanism when such a threshold is reached.
sections.plainLanguage: A central server that can program every router is a valuable target, so the document says to run these sessions over encrypted, mutually authenticated connections between systems under the same administration. It also warns that a rogue server could flood a router with instructions, and that a server must limit how much state a single router can make it keep.

sections.title: The Registries This Document Adds To
sections.content:
Several registries gain new entries. In the PATH-SETUP-TYPE-CAPABILITY Sub-TLV Type Indicators subregistry, IANA allocated the codepoint 1 for the PCECC-CAPABILITY sub-TLV. A new subregistry manages the 32-bit Flag field of that sub-TLV, with new values assigned by Standards Action; bits 0 to 30 are unassigned and bit 31 is the Label bit.

In the PCEP Path Setup Types subregistry, the value 2 was allocated for a traffic engineering path set up using PCECC mode. In the PCEP Objects subregistry, the CCI object was allocated Object-Class 44, with Object-Type 0 reserved, Object-Type 1 for the MPLS label and Object-Types 2 to 15 unassigned. A new subregistry manages the Flag field of the CCI object for MPLS label, again with new values assigned by Standards Action: bits 0 to 13 are unassigned, bit 14 is the C bit for PCC allocation and bit 15 is the O bit that specifies the label is the out-label.

Finally, new error types and values were added to the PCEP-ERROR Object Error Types and Values subregistry. Error-Type 6, Mandatory Object missing, gains value 17 for a missing CCI object. Error-Type 10, Reception of an invalid object, gains value 33 for a missing PCECC Capability sub-TLV. Error-Type 19, Invalid Operation, gains value 16 for attempted PCECC operations when the capability was not advertised, value 17 for the stateful PCE capability not being advertised and value 18 for an unknown label. Error-Type 31, PCECC failure, gains value 1 for a label out of range, value 2 for a failed instruction, value 3 for an invalid CCI, value 4 for being unable to allocate the specified CCI and value 5 for invalid next-hop information.
sections.plainLanguage: The document asks the Internet registry for a few new numbers: a new path setup type, a new object type, two new flag bits and a set of error codes. These are the numbers an implementation has to put on the wire.

fields.name: CC-ID
fields.desc: PCEP-specific identifier for the instruction, unique within the PCE and constant for the session.

fields.name: Reserved1
fields.desc: Set to zero while sending; ignored on receipt.

fields.name: Flags
fields.desc: Bit 15 is the O bit for the out-label; bit 14 is the C bit for PCC allocation.

fields.name: Reserved2
fields.desc: Set to zero while sending; ignored on receipt.
